title: Mock 1 · Foundations
blurb: Core definitions plus first-step numericals: contract value, basis, carry, IV, BEP and bonus adjustment.

questions.q: Which derivative can best be described as an 'exchange-traded, standardised forward contract'?
questions.explanation: The workbook says futures are similar to forwards except that they are standardised (lot size, maturity, etc.) and traded on an organised exchange. Hence 'futures are exchange traded forward contracts'.
hints: A swap is a series of forward contracts exchanging cash flows; it is OTC.
Correct: a futures contract is a standardised forward traded on an exchange.
A forward is customised and OTC, not standardised or exchange-traded.
An option gives a right without obligation; it is not a forward.

questions.q: A participant buys a share on one exchange and simultaneously sells it on another at a higher price to lock in a risk-free gain. This participant is a/an:
questions.explanation: Arbitrage exploits a price difference for the same product in two markets by buying cheap and selling dear simultaneously. Such opportunities close quickly as arbitrageurs rush in.
hints: A hedger uses derivatives to reduce an existing risk, not to exploit price gaps.
A speculator takes a directional view and bears risk.
Correct: simultaneous buy-low/sell-high across markets is arbitrage.
A writer is the seller of an option, an unrelated role.

questions.q: A price-weighted index has four stocks priced at ₹120, ₹80, ₹200 and ₹100. What is the index value?
questions.explanation: Price index = sum of prices / number of stocks = (120 + 80 + 200 + 100) / 4 = 500 / 4 = 125.
hints: 500 is only the sum of prices; you must divide by the number of stocks.
100 is just one stock's price.
150 does not follow from the formula.

questions.q: Nifty futures trade at 24,500 and the lot size is 75. What is the value of one futures contract?
questions.explanation: Contract value = futures price × lot size = 24,500 × 75 = ₹18,37,500. This is within SEBI's ₹15–20 lakh band for index derivatives.
hints: Off by a factor of 10.
You added the lot size instead of multiplying.
You divided instead of multiplying.

questions.q: A stock trades at ₹1,200 in the cash market and its near-month futures at ₹1,212. As defined in the workbook, the basis is:
questions.explanation: Basis = Spot − Futures = 1,200 − 1,212 = −12. When futures trade above spot, the basis is negative.
hints: The sign is wrong: the workbook defines basis as spot minus futures.
Basis is zero only at expiry, when prices converge.
Basis is an absolute difference, and here it is negative.

questions.q: A trader buys one stock futures contract at ₹2,450 (lot size 500) and squares off at ₹2,410. What is the result?
questions.explanation: Long futures P&L = (exit − entry) × lot = (2,410 − 2,450) × 500 = −40 × 500 = −₹20,000, a loss.
hints: A long position loses when the price falls.
The decimal is wrong: 40 × 500 = 20,000.
Both the sign and the amount are wrong.

questions.q: A share trades at ₹200. An investor can borrow at 9% p.a. and expects a dividend of ₹4 over the next year. Using the simple cost-of-carry logic in the workbook, the break-even one-year futures price is:
questions.explanation: Net carry = interest − dividend = (9% × 200) − 4 = 18 − 4 = ₹14. Break-even futures = 200 + 14 = ₹214.
hints: You ignored the interest and only added the dividend.
You ignored the dividend inflow, which reduces carry.
You subtracted the dividend from spot without adding interest.

questions.q: In an exchange-traded futures contract, initial margin has to be deposited by:
options: Both the buyer and the seller
questions.explanation: Both parties to a futures contract have an obligation, so both buyer and seller pay initial margin.
hints: The seller also has an obligation and must pay margin.
The buyer also has an obligation and must pay margin.
The clearing corporation collects margins; it does not pay them.
Correct: both sides are obligated, so both pay margin.

questions.q: A stock trades at ₹540. The 500-strike call is quoted at ₹52. What is the intrinsic value of the call?
questions.explanation: Call intrinsic value = max(S − X, 0) = 540 − 500 = ₹40. The remaining 52 − 40 = ₹12 is time value.
hints: ₹52 is the full premium (intrinsic + time value).
₹12 is the time value, not the intrinsic value.
The call is in the money, so its intrinsic value is not zero.

questions.q: You buy a put with a strike of ₹300 at a premium of ₹18. Your break-even price at expiry is:
questions.explanation: Put BEP = Strike − Premium = 300 − 18 = ₹282. Below 282 the long put makes a net profit.
hints: Strike + premium is the BEP for a call, not a put.
At the strike, the put buyer loses the full premium.
You subtracted the premium twice.

questions.q: Index and stock options traded on Indian exchanges are of which exercise style?
questions.explanation: The workbook states: 'In India, all index and stock options are European style options', so they can be exercised only on the expiry day.
hints: American options allow exercise any time up to expiry; India does not use them.
Correct: all Indian index and stock options are European.
Bermudan style is not covered and not used.
Asian (average-price) options are not exchange-traded in Indian equity F&O.

questions.q: What is the maximum possible loss for the buyer of a call option?
questions.explanation: A long option position has limited risk: at worst the buyer lets the option lapse and loses the premium paid. Profit potential is unlimited.
hints: Correct: the buyer's loss is capped at the premium.
Unlimited loss applies to the call writer, not the buyer.
The buyer never loses the strike; he just doesn't exercise.
This overstates the risk; only the premium is at stake.

questions.q: A stock is at ₹1,050. Which of the following put options is out-of-the-money?
questions.explanation: A put is OTM when the spot price is above the strike. Only the 1,000 strike satisfies S (1,050) > X.
hints: Correct: S > X, so the 1,000 put is OTM.
S < X, so this put is in the money.
S < X, so this put is in the money.
S < X, so this put is in the money.

questions.q: An investor buys a call with a lower strike and sells a call with a higher strike on the same stock and expiry. This strategy is a:
questions.explanation: A bull (vertical) call spread is long the lower-strike call and short the higher-strike call. It starts with a net debit and has limited profit and limited loss.
hints: A bear call spread sells the lower strike and buys the higher strike.
Correct: long lower-strike call + short higher-strike call = bull call spread.
A straddle uses a call and a put at the same strike.
A butterfly needs three strikes (1 long, 2 short, 1 long).

questions.q: A trader buys a 500-strike call at ₹22 and a 500-strike put at ₹18, both with the same expiry. What are the two break-even points?
questions.explanation: Long straddle BEPs = Strike ± total premium = 500 ± (22 + 18) = 460 and 540. The maximum loss is ₹40, at a price of 500.
hints: This uses only the call premium (22).
This uses only the put premium (18).
500 is where the maximum loss occurs, not a BEP.
Correct: 500 ± 40 = 460 and 540.

questions.q: Put open interest on an index is 15,000 contracts and call open interest is 12,000. What is the PCR and how is it usually read?
questions.explanation: PCR = Put OI / Call OI = 15,000 / 12,000 = 1.25. As a contrarian indicator, PCR > 1 is taken as bullish (option sellers do not expect a fall).
hints: Ratio inverted; PCR is puts divided by calls.
Correct: 1.25, read as bullish.
The ratio is right but the reading is wrong; PCR > 1 is bullish.
The ratio is inverted and the reading is mismatched.

questions.q: An order that is matched as soon as it is released into the system, with any unmatched portion cancelled immediately, is a/an:
questions.explanation: An IOC order allows partial matching, and the unmatched portion is cancelled immediately.
hints: A day order remains valid until the end of the day.
A stop-loss order waits for a trigger price.
Correct: IOC executes at once, and the rest is cancelled.
A limit order sits in the book until filled at the limit or better.

questions.q: A company announces a 1:1 bonus. A stock option has a strike of ₹800 and a market lot of 400. What are the adjusted strike and lot?
questions.explanation: Bonus A:B gives an adjustment factor (A+B)/B = (1+1)/1 = 2. New strike = 800/2 = 400; new lot = 400 × 2 = 800. The position value is preserved.
hints: Correct: strike ÷ 2 and lot × 2.
Corporate actions are adjusted so that the value stays the same; the figures cannot stay unchanged.
Lot must increase when the strike falls.
Adjusted in the wrong direction.

questions.q: As per the rates effective from April 1, 2026 in the workbook, STT on the sale of a futures contract is:
options: 0.15% of traded value, paid by the buyer
0.1% of traded value, paid by both
0.15% of traded value, paid by the seller
0.05% of the traded price, paid by the seller
questions.explanation: STT on the sale of futures in securities is 0.05%, payable by the seller on the price at which the futures is traded.
hints: 0.15% applies to options, and the buyer pays only on exercise.
0.1% on both sides applies to delivery-based equity (physical settlement).
0.15% is the option-premium rate, not the futures rate.
Correct: 0.05%, paid by the seller.

questions.q: The legal principle by which the clearing corporation becomes the central counterparty to every trade is called:
questions.explanation: Under novation, the clearing corporation becomes the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer, and guarantees settlement.
hints: Netting offsets obligations; it does not substitute the counterparty.
Correct: novation makes the CC the central counterparty.
Assignment allocates exercised options to writers.
Margining is a risk-control tool, not counterparty substitution.

questions.q: Since October 2019, positions in futures and options on individual stocks that remain open on expiry are settled by:
options: The buyer's choice of cash or delivery
questions.explanation: Since October 2019, all open positions in stock F&O on expiry are settled by physical delivery. Index F&O continue to be cash-settled.
hints: Cash settlement applies to index F&O.
No such choice exists.
Correct: stock F&O are physically settled.
Auction is not the settlement method.

questions.q: The Market-Wide Position Limit (MWPL) for F&O on an individual security is:
options: 20% of the shares held by non-promoters (free float)
questions.explanation: MWPL = 20% of the number of shares held by non-promoters, i.e., 20% of free float in number of shares.
hints: Correct: 20% of free-float shares.
Neither the percentage nor the base is correct.
15% relates to TM index limits and the OI disclosure threshold.
1% of free float is part of the client-level limit.

questions.q: Which provision of the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 makes derivative contracts legal and valid if they are traded on a recognised stock exchange and settled through its clearing house?
questions.explanation: Section 18A of SCRA provides that derivative contracts are legal and valid if traded on a recognised stock exchange and settled through its clearing house.
hints: Section 2(h) defines 'securities'.
Section 4 concerns recognition of stock exchanges.
Correct: Section 18A.
Section 43(5) is an Income-tax Act provision on speculative transactions.

questions.q: For a resident individual, profits from equity derivatives traded on a recognised stock exchange are taxed as:
questions.explanation: Finance Act 2005 amended Section 43(5) to exclude derivatives on recognised exchanges from speculative transactions. Such income is non-speculative income under 'Profits and Gains from Business or Profession'.
hints: This was the position only before FY 2005-06.
Capital gains treatment applies to FPIs, not resident traders.
F&O income is not 'other sources'.
Correct: non-speculative business income.

questions.q: Under AML/CFT regulations, suspicious transactions must be reported to:
options: The stock exchange's investor grievance cell
questions.explanation: Suspicious transactions are reported to FIU-IND, set up by the Government to detect money laundering attempts.
hints: Correct: STRs go to FIU-IND.
RBI is not the STR recipient for brokers.
CVC deals with vigilance in government bodies.
The grievance cell handles investor complaints, not STRs.
